findings.title: Returned Connection* is a borrowed pointer with an undocumented keep-alive / use-after-close contract
findings.description: extract_connection_ptr returns conn_ptr (line 74) as a bare Python int read from offset +32 inside the C++ DuckDBPyConnection (line 62). This int is a *borrowed* raw pointer: the underlying Connection is owned by the Python `conn` object (the unique_ptr<Connection> living inside the pybind11 instance). A Python int cannot hold `conn` referenced, so the pointer is only valid while `conn` is alive AND open. The docstring's Returns section (lines 41-43) documents only 'The Connection* as a Python int (intp-compatible)' and says nothing about this borrow. This is the exact invariant the sibling numbox bridge — which this file is explicitly modeled on — spells out in dedicated Returns + Warning sections (numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py:129-144: 'borrowed from conn ... stays valid only while conn is alive and open ... must not use the pointer after conn.close() or after conn is garbage-collected — doing so is a use-after-free'). The omission is a real memory-safety documentation gap, not a behavioral bug: the borrow design itself is correct.
findings.impact: A downstream caller who writes `ptr = extract_connection_ptr(duckdb.connect())` (not retaining the connection), or who uses the pointer after `conn.close()` / after `conn` is GC'd, dereferences a dangling `Connection*` inside @njit duckdb_* calls — a silent use-after-free / segfault. In-repo callers (examples/*.py, test/test_ducklib.py) all keep `conn` in a live local, so no current crash; the risk is for external API consumers who lack the warning.
findings.recommendation: Add to the docstring the same borrowed-pointer contract the sibling documents: state in Returns that the pointer is borrowed from and owned by `conn`, and add a Warning that the caller must retain `conn` (alive and open) for the entire lifetime of any @njit use of the returned pointer, and must not use it after conn.close() or GC.

findings.title: No null/validity guard on the extracted pointer before it is dereferenced by the SELECT 1 validation
findings.description: conn_ptr is read from `cpp_obj_p + 32` (line 62) and passed straight into ducklib.duckdb_query(conn_ptr, ...) (line 67) with no check that it is non-null or live. The sibling bridge explicitly guards this: `if db_ptr is None: raise RuntimeError('extracted null sqlite3* ...')` (numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py:169-170). Two concrete failure modes follow from the missing guard: (a) if the unique_ptr<Connection> slot at +32 is null (e.g. a closed or not-yet-connected DuckDBPyConnection), ctypes' `c_void_p(...).value` yields Python None, and duckdb_query(None, ...) then fails as an uninformative numba typing TypeError at dispatch — not the RuntimeError the docstring promises (lines 49-50); and worse, if cpp_obj_p itself is null, `cpp_obj_p + 32` on line 62 raises `TypeError: unsupported operand ... NoneType + int`. (b) The SELECT 1 'validation' (lines 64-72) is validation-by-dereference: for a stale/dangling non-null pointer (closed connection, or an ABI/layout drift on a different duckdb build that still passes the isinstance guard at lines 52-55), duckdb_query dereferences the bad Connection* — that is already undefined behavior / a segfault BEFORE any rc can be returned, so the check cannot protect against an invalid pointer, only report a live-but-erroring one.
findings.impact: Calling extract_connection_ptr on a closed/uninitialized connection produces a confusing TypeError instead of the documented RuntimeError, and on a dangling (freed-but-non-null) Connection* it is a use-after-free / segfault inside duckdb_query. The docstring claim that the pointer 'is validated ... before it is returned' overstates the guarantee.
findings.recommendation: Before the validation query, guard the extracted pointers the way the sibling does: after line 59 check that cpp_obj_p is not None (raise RuntimeError on a null holder), and after line 62 check `if conn_ptr is None: raise RuntimeError('extracted null Connection* from DuckDBPyConnection')`. Optionally document that the SELECT 1 check only distinguishes live-but-failing from success and cannot catch a structurally invalid pointer.

notes: Aspects checked and found SOUND (no defect): (1) conn lifetime/GC during the raw reads — `conn` is held in the function's local for the whole call and CPython never moves objects, so id(conn) and the +16/+32 from_address reads are stable; no GC/move hazard. (2) Validation query leak/double-free — duckdb_destroy_result(result.ctypes.data) is called exactly once and unconditionally BEFORE the rc check (lines 68-69), and duckdb_query populates the result struct on both success and error, so the internal_data is freed on every path with no leak and no double-free. (3) numpy result buffer alive across the C call — `result` (create_duckdb_result() -> numpy.zeros(6,int64) = 48 bytes, exact size of the 6-field duckdb_result in the whole >=1.3.2,<1.6 pin) is retained in a local for both the duckdb_query and duckdb_destroy_result calls, so .ctypes.data stays backed. (4) get_unicode_data_p("SELECT 1") lifetime — verified against numba cpython/unicode.py unbox_unicode_str (lines 178-197): the returned int aliases the CPython str's own data buffer (not an NRT copy). The "SELECT 1" literal is a co_consts constant of extract_connection_ptr's code object, so it outlives the whole call; query_p stays valid across duckdb_query. NOT a dangling pointer, despite the understanding-note flag. pybridge.py touches no borrow_structref/release_meminfo/export_meminfo, so there is no meminfo refcount balance concern in this unit. Latent (not a current defect, belongs to duckdb_utils.py): create_duckdb_result hard-codes 48 bytes; if any in-pin duckdb release grew duckdb_result past 48 bytes, duckdb_query would OOB-write the numpy buffer — the struct has been 48 bytes across 1.3.x-1.5.x, so no current issue. Both findings above are deviations from the established sibling contract in numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py, which numbduck's pybridge is explicitly modeled on.
